chapter: Piano influences and the New Orleans scene
title: Late 1930s: Father Toots and learning from many pianists
summary: He recalls a floor show around 1938-40, the helper Father Toots and a piano player in Stormy Weather, and says he built his piano style by combining many players.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: 19th. What time was that, uh, uh, uh, we were working at the New York Antis. You know, when we had that little flow show.
Mmm. That was in the 50s. What was it?
Oh, that was in the 50s. I was in the 80s.
New York Antis. Down here. Uh-huh.
That was a pro-roar. Oh, yeah. That was around 40. Rowland was around 42, around 40 and 41. Around 40? Around 39 and 40.

Yeah, somewhere around there. 38 to 39. And another little fella used to give me a hand, his name was Father Toots. He's still around somewhere around here. Around Jefferson, C.S.B.R. or Seasbury someplace. He's good too.
You know his real name? What his regular name is?

That name used so long, if we called his real name he wouldn't always know it. We'd all call him Father Toots. And we had another little fella in the stormy weather. He was good, but he's dead too. What did he play? Piano.

Well I managed to mix up the real baddest fellas, you know, playing piano. That's why I learned to develop so well, because I learned so many different actions and changes and cross-cord by listening to one through the other. I said well I take them all and put them in the sack together so I play a little bit of all of their music, plus what I can think of myself. And that's how I learned how to play piano.
